prize_parts.citation: For founding the intertemporal, microfounded approach to open-economy macroeconomics and for identifying the exchange-rate and related puzzles that still structure the field.

statement.case_for: Obstfeld and Rogoff made open-economy macroeconomics an intertemporal, microfounded field. Their Redux model and joint textbook supplied the standard framework for analysing current accounts, exchange rates and international spillovers. They also framed the exchange-rate disconnect and related puzzles, which continue to organise research. Credit is concentrated in two people with a clearly joint programme, so a two-name citation is clean. The work is three decades old and has been absorbed into academic and policy practice, and international macroeconomics has not been recognised recently. After reading colleagues' arguments I still rank this first on contribution, attribution and maturity. Candidates with broader opening support have strong scientific cases too, but support counts are not evidence of merit and did not move my ranking.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the contribution is partly a research agenda rather than a settled result. Several of the named puzzles remain unresolved. The price-setting assumptions in the Redux model have limited empirical support. A committee could also see the work as a rigorous extension of the Mundell-Fleming tradition rather than a distinct discovery. The attribution of the puzzles is less clean than that of the framework, because Sachs, Svensson, Corsetti, Gopinath and others contributed to adjacent strands. Opening support is thin compared with the leading trade and labour candidates.

responses.point: Andersson ranks the Obstfeld-Rogoff framework second. He credits it with founding the modern intertemporal approach and framing the disconnect puzzles. He cautions that unresolved puzzles make the discovery partly an agenda, and that Rogoff's other work could shape how the committee frames the credit.
responses.response: I agree the puzzles are an agenda rather than a result, and I would not rest the citation on them. The prize case is the framework: the intertemporal current-account approach and the Redux synthesis, which have a three-decade record of use in teaching, central banks and the IMF. The puzzles are the part of the contribution that is still alive. I would draft the citation to credit the framework first and the puzzles second, and keep Rogoff's separate work outside the credited contribution. That keeps the attribution to what the two did jointly.

responses.point: Friberg ranks it fourth and calls it a pillar of international macroeconomics. He notes that attribution of the puzzles is less clean than that of the framework. He also says the empirical relevance of the Redux price-setting assumptions is limited.
responses.response: I accept both qualifications. The puzzles have several originators, and the Redux sticky-price specification is not what current open-economy models rely on empirically. But the Nobel standard here is originating a framework that reorganised a field, not the long-run empirical success of one specification. The intertemporal budget-constraint discipline and the microfounded welfare analysis have survived the specific nominal-rigidity assumptions and are what later work builds on. That separates the durable core from the vulnerable part, and it is why I limit the credit to the two names that jointly founded the framework.

responses.point: Hassler ranks Grossman and Helpman first. He argues their protection-for-sale work and their growth-and-trade work are general, influential across fields, mature, and cleanly attributed to two people.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution and maturity case for Grossman and Helpman is strong, and it is a serious alternative. Two things keep me from ranking it first. The ballot's stated discovery is trade-policy political economy, where empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed. And the innovation-and-growth strand overlaps with the 2025 growth prize. I would rather not rest a prize on a strand the Academy has just recognised. Helpman's role in the firm-heterogeneity ballot also means a choice between the two trade lines would need to be made explicitly, not by default.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the intertemporal open-economy framework as a distinct discovery or as an extension of Mundell-Fleming.
How much weight the unresolved exchange-rate puzzles should carry in a citation, given several originators.

If the committee prefers a trade prize, whether it should be anchored on political economy (B001) or on firm heterogeneity (B030). The two share Helpman, and Bernard, Eaton and Kortum are omitted from B030.
My opening view on B001 was limited. I did not rank it, and I have not independently verified its empirical record beyond general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred configuration (Obstfeld, Rogoff) from the supplied profile. For disclosure on other ballots, Peter Klenow, credited on B037, is a long-running co-author of mine. I ranked B037 sixth, and it is not in my proposal. I am also an associate professor at IIES and a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and John Hassler, and I have co-authored with Philippe Aghion. None of these links bears directly on the credited names in my proposal.
